cues.text: Is bluffing in poker actually a good idea, mathematically? Or is it just psychology?
Let's find out, with a tiny version of poker that's small enough to solve exactly.
There are four cards, one through four. Each player gets one card, and the higher card wins.
Each player has four chips.
The first player puts in a small blind of one chip, and the second player puts in a big blind of two chips.
Now the small blind can fold, or call by putting in one more chip, or raise all-in, to four chips.
If the small blind raises, the big blind can fold or call.
If the small blind calls, the big blind can check, and we see who wins, or it can raise all-in, and then the small blind can fold or call.
And that's the whole game. At the end of each branch, we can write how many chips the small blind wins or loses.
Now, a strategy is a plan for what to do with each card you might get.
The small blind has four plans for each card: fold, raise, call and then fold, or call and then call. Four choices for each of four cards is four to the fourth, or 256 strategies.
The big blind also has two decisions for each card, with two options each, so also 256 strategies.
If we pick a strategy for each player, we can work out the average payoff by playing out all twelve ways the cards can be dealt.
Doing that for every pair of strategies gives us a 256 by 256 payoff matrix. Green is good for the small blind, and red is bad.
Now, the small blind doesn't have to pick just one strategy. It can choose a probability for each one: a vector of 256 weights that add up to one.
The big blind does the same, and the small blind's average payoff is x, times the matrix, times y.
Let's be pessimistic, and assume the big blind knows our weights, and picks its best response.
Then we want the weights that make our worst case as good as possible. That's a linear program: maximize v, so that every column gives us at least v.
When we solve it, out of 256 strategies, just three get used, each one third of the time.
And no matter what the big blind does, the small blind wins at least five thirty-sixths of a chip per hand, on average.
Let's turn that into a human strategy. With a four, always raise. With a three, call, and if the big blind raises, call two thirds of the time. With a two, fold.
And with a one, the worst card, fold two thirds of the time, but one third of the time, raise all-in. That's a bluff!
The big blind bluffs too. With a one, if the small blind just calls, it raises one third of the time.
But why one third? Imagine you're the big blind, holding a three, and the small blind raises.
The small blind raises with every four, and with a third of its ones. So a quarter of its raises are bluffs.
If you fold, you lose two chips. If you call, you win four chips a quarter of the time, and lose four chips three quarters of the time. That's also losing two, on average.
So calling and folding are equally good. The bluffs are exactly frequent enough that the big blind can't tell what to do.
If the small blind never bluffs, then a raise always means a four, so the big blind just folds, and the small blind's payoff drops to four thirty-sixths.
And if the big blind isn't allowed to bluff, the small blind's payoff jumps all the way up to twelve thirty-sixths.
So bluffing isn't just psychology. Even in this tiny game, the mathematically best strategy bluffs, with exactly the right frequency.
